UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                            BEFORE THE
               FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                       )
PJM Interconnection, et al.            )       Docket No. EL25-49-000, et al.
                                       )

    LIMITED REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF PUBLIC INTEREST
                      ORGANIZATIONS

      Pursuant to Section 313 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”),1 and Rules 212
and 713 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,2 Earthjustice,
Environmental Defense Fund, and Sierra Club (Public Interest Organizations)
request clarification of the Commission’s December 18, 2025 order in the above-
captioned proceeding, 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“Order”), pursuant to the reasons
more fully described below.

       I.     Background

       Last February, the Commission took on the tough task of prompting PJM to
revisit its processes for addressing large load arrangements.3 As part of the show
cause proceeding, the Commission sought feedback from PJM and stakeholders on
over thirty comprehensive briefing questions covering topic areas that required
further clarity to support colocation arrangements, including cost allocation for
transmission service4 and resource adequacy concerns, such as whether PJM should
consider changes to its “planning processes” or “load forecasting methods” to “better
plan for and address resource adequacy and reliability impacts of co-location
arrangements.”5

      The Commission’s Show Cause Order specifically asked whether PJM should
“consider changes to load forecasting methods, informational postings, or the
reserve margin study process to better plan for and address the resource adequacy
and reliability impacts of co-location arrangements.”6 As further detailed below, on

 April 23, 2025, Public Interest Organizations (PIOs) filed comments that
comprehensively responded to, among other things, this question.7 On September
18, 2025, Commissioner Rosner issued a follow-up letter to PJM specifically
requesting information relating to PJM’s existing process and future expectations
regarding its load forecasting process.8 PJM responded to that letter on October 17,
2025.9

       Based on the responses to its Show Cause Order, the Commission issued a
decision on December 18, 2025.10 While we agree that the Order takes several
measures to ensure that rates are just and reasonable for consumers,11 it is unclear
how the timing and format of some of the measures will serve their stated purpose,
and if so, whether they will be implemented in a timely manner. As explained in
our response, certain prerequisite revisions to PJM’s planning processes, like
reformed load forecasting procedures, are necessary before PJM can serve large
loads using its existing transmission services and its processes for forecasting
capacity market demand and planning regional transmission projects (RTEP) while
maintaining rates that are just and reasonable.12

      II.    Limited Request for Clarification

             A. We request clarification on how the rates for PJM’s
                Commission-jurisdictional services will be just and
                reasonable during the interim period before PJM
                implements procedures to avoid using speculative load
                information

             1. Accurate demand forecasts are needed to support imminent
             phases of PJM’s next capacity market and RTEP processes

       PJM’s RTEP and capacity market processes are in the midst of using PJM’s
load forecasts to plan system needs that will drive energy infrastructure
investments and impact wholesale electricity rates. PJM is preparing to hold the

at 15-24 (filed Apr. 23, 2025) (hereinafter “PIO Comments”).
8 See Commissioner Rosner, Letter to PJM, Docket Nos. EL25-49, et al. (Sept. 18,

2025) (“Rosner Letter”).
9 See Asthana, Manu, Letter in Response, Docket No. EL25-49, et al., (Oct. 17,

2025), available at: https://www.ferc.gov/media/pjm-response-chairman-david-
rosners-09192025-letter-re-large-load-forecasting-americas. (“PJM October Letter”).
10 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (Order).
11 Order P 162; see also Rosner Concurrence P 1.
12 PIO Comments at 6, 20.


                                         2
 next Base Residual Auction in June 2026.13 The auction will rely in part on PJM’s
demand forecast. With respect to the RTEP, PJM will use data that it gathers from
November 2025 through March 2026 to build base case modeling assumptions and
perform initial case reviews.14 And from March 2026 to June 2026, PJM expects to
perform its RTEP baseline studies,15 which will inform the transmission projects
that will be available in the competitive bidding window that PJM expects to open
in July 2026.

             2. Without a specific directive, PJM is not likely to resolve the
             issues with its forecasting process in a timely manner

       In the Order, the Commission did not directly address the load forecasting
issues raised in the record; however, the Commission did require PJM to provide an
informational filing that includes, among other things, an update regarding the
development of “enhanced load forecasting.”16 Here, we request clarification
regarding how the Commission intends to respond to, or otherwise use, the
information provided in the record, and any additional information provided by
PJM pursuant to the Commission’s request in any subsequent order related to this
series of dockets.17 The issues raised by PIOs merit immediate consideration
because of the way in which large load forecasting impacts whether the outcome of
the newly proposed colocation transmission service pathways ultimately result in
rates that are just and reasonable.

      Specifically, in our comments we noted that, “PJM’s Tariff is unjust and
unreasonable because it lacks sufficient controls and standards to ensure large load
forecast accuracy and to protect against speculative large load forecast estimates.”18
We argued that “PJM’s large load forecasting process does not substantively
account for speculative load additions, thus rendering the process and resulting
forecast, as well as everything that relies on that forecast, unjust and

https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/newsroom/2025-

assumptions.pdf.

informational Filing.” Order P 238, n.486.

 unreasonable,” and also that PJM’s failure to include the provisions governing large
load forecasting in the PJM Tariff violates the Commission’s Rule of Reason.19

      PJM’s load forecasting procedure can largely be found on three pages in PJM
Manual 19, attachment B.20 We identified four primary problems with PJM’s
current process. First, the LSE/EDCs in PJM report their large load forecasts in
completely different ways, posing a substantial gradient in uncertainty based on the
standards and criteria each participant uses in submitting its forecast to PJM.21
Second, PJM has no way to cross-check whether a data center in, for example,
Exelon’s service territory has also made the same proposal in Dominion’s territory,
and both proposals end up in PJM’s forecast even though only one will be built.22
Third, PJM’s process has no way to timely ensure that large data center
cancellations are quickly identified and incorporated into PJM’s forecasts.23 Lastly,
we contend that because PJM’s large load forecasting processes are not codified in
PJM’s Tariff, and they directly and significantly affect rates for jurisdictional
Commission services, their omission violates the Commission’s Rule of Reason.24 We
predicted that the combination of these four problems will necessarily result in
highly uncertain, and likely inflated load forecasts that will result in unjust and
unreasonable rates.

      In addition to the question posed in the Show Cause Order, as noted above,
Commissioner Rosner submitted a letter to PJM on September 18, 2025, noting that
“we cannot efficiently plan the electric generation and transmission needed to serve
new customers if we don’t forecast how much energy they will need as accurately as
possible.”25 Commissioner Rosner then posed a series of questions for PJM to
answer that are largely consistent with the issues raised in PIOs’ comments:

         (1) How do you, the utilities in your footprint, and state regulators obtain
         information that verifies when and whether prospective large loads in your
         region will reach commercial operation?
         (2) To what extent are prospective large load requests subject to consistent,
         objective screening criteria before they are included in the load forecast?
         (3) How do you forecast how the actual electricity consumption of a large load
         will compare to its requested level of interconnection service?

        (4) How do you coordinate with utilities at the regional or interregional level
       to share best practices on large load forecasting and ensure that large load
       interconnection requests are not double-counted?26

        On October 17, 2025, PJM responded to Commissioner Rosner’s letter.27 PJM
also indicated that it has adopted a Load Adjustment Request Implementation
document that “offers enhanced transparency about PJM’s load adjustment request
submission process in PJM Manual 19, Attachment B.”28 With regard to PIOs’
comments, while the document specifies generally what types of information PJM
desires from forecast submitters and explains a basic weighting criteria, it expressly
does not require or “specify a particular methodology for forecasting large loads.”29
Without a clear methodology, LSE/EDCs will continue to report data with widely
varying accuracy, which will necessarily result in uncertain forecasts.
Commissioner Rosner also asked PJM to respond to the concern of double-counting
of data centers; however, PJM’s response does not identify a concrete way in which
it is currently, or plans to in the future, address this issue. Instead, it merely
concludes that PJM “looks forward to continued collaboration with its stakeholders .
. . to pursue additional enhancements and opportunities for consistency across the
region.”30 This response is not sufficient to address this well-known issue across the
industry.31 Additionally, nothing in PJM’s response addresses the need for more
timely updates to the load forecasting process in PJM. Considering the way in
which significant load proposals are dropped, or added, PJM needs a more dynamic
approach for updating the load forecasts to reflect the current state of demand.32
Thus, it is unclear how the informational report on PJM’s activities that the
Commission directed in the Order will ensure PJM implements needed
improvements to its process in a timely manner.

               3. The inaccuracy of PJM’s demand forecasting was recently
               demonstrated

        Unfortunately, PIOs’ concerns regarding the accuracy of PJM’s load forecasts
have recently been actualized. PJM’s recent announcements call into question the
accuracy of the inputs to PJM’s most recent capacity market auction and related
wholesale electricity market rates as well as its transmission planning models.
Shortly after PJM’s 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction, Stu Bresler, PJM’s former
Executive Vice President of Market Services and Strategy, indicated during a press
conference that the 2026 Forecast would likely reflect a decrease in forecasted load
for that time period since PJM is revising its process for implementing load
adjustments.33 However, that course correction came too late for ratepayers. As a
reminder, the 2027/2028 auction resulted in a capacity shortfall and “record [high]
prices” in part due to the projected demand, which included 5,100 MW for data
centers. Regarding the next auction, PJM Chief Operating Officer Stu Bresler said
that “PJM’s overall power demand forecast for the year beginning in mid-2027 will
be ‘appreciably lower’ than current projections.”34 According to PJM’s most recent
2026 PJM Load Forecast Report, its most recent analysis has “brought large load
adjustments down in the near-term forecast years compared to the 2025 Long-Term
Load Forecast.”35

      State representatives and industry experts are also sounding the alarms.36
Former NARUC President, Travis Kavula, has stated that despite PJM now
“applying a scintilla of judgment,” its forecast “remains a colossal act of
speculation.”37 Considering that PJM uses its load forecasts to essentially set the
demand curve for capacity obligations, for reliability studies, and to support the

“colossally” inaccurate, how can the resulting rates from these processes be just and
reasonable without significant revisions to PJM’s process?

      We request clarification regarding how the Commission intends to use the
informational report directed in its Decision,39 and further request that any
subsequent order from the Commission address the issues raised in the record
regarding the continuing and ongoing deficiencies in PJM’s large load forecasting
process.

             B. Evaluating whether the status quo transmission rate design
                for large load customers is still just and reasonable

       Given the unprecedented volume and scale of large-load requests, the
Commission should evaluate whether existing transmission rate designs remain
just and reasonable. In the Order, the Commission determined that co-located load
paying for NITS service would be responsible for costs that are at least "roughly
commensurate" with benefits because zonal NITS rates include upgrades and
operations and maintenance costs.40 However, this rate design relies on a standard
that assumes load growth is incremental and widely distributed.
       The practical reality is that discrete large-load pockets trigger multi-million-
dollar reliability solutions. Because customers pay only in proportion to billing
determinants (usage shares) rather than incremental costs triggered, a significant
“payer gap” can emerged. Under Schedule 12 of the PJM Tariff, a substantial share
of the revenue requirement for RTEP projects are allocated regionally through the
Transmission Enhancement Charge.41 For example, the Mars-Golden-Lockridge
Complex (2022 RTEP Window 3) is now estimated at $725.3M following April 2025
scope updates. Under a 7% load-share illustrative, the triggering load pays only
$50.8M, leaving $674.5M to be socialized among other customers.
      The gap is even more pronounced in the Southern Cluster / “Kraken”
package—a $5.08B portfolio centered on a 185-mile undergrounded HVDC line
approved in the 2024 RTEP Window 1 to serve “Data Center Alley.”42 If a 1,000 MW

 data center represents 7% of the zone’s peak determinants, it contributes only
$203M, leaving a $4.877B gap for unrelated regional and zonal customers.
       The Commission has already recognized the need for a departure from the
status quo allocation in other contexts. In its October 10, 2025 approval of SPP’s
Provisional Load Process (Docket No. ER25-2430), the Commission accepted a cost
causation approach that initially assigns upgrade costs to transmission customers
to protect existing users from “the uncertain nature of load and generation
additions.”43
       Accordingly, we request that the Commission clarify how “roughly
commensurate” is evaluated when a discrete driver’s pro-rata contribution is
dwarfed by the multi-billion-dollar infrastructure it necessitates. Furthermore, the
Commission should direct PJM and its Transmission Owners to provide
transparent reporting for major projects that explicitly compares incremental cost
causation against pro-rata billing determinant recovery, ensuring the resulting
allocation is not unjust and unreasonable, or unduly discriminatory or preferential.

        III.   Conclusion

      For the foregoing reasons, Earthjustice, Environmental Defense Fund, and
Sierra Club respectfully request that the Commission clarify its December 18, 2025
Order.
